newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Singapore libel case sends chill through Asia.
newsitem.headline: Singapore libel case sends chill through Asia.

text.p: Record libel damages won by Singapore's prime minister and senior colleagues on Thursday sent a chill through Asia and legal experts said the ruling exposed a gap between the city-state's economic and political development.

A Singapore court awarded Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and 10 senior members of the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) a record S$8.08 million (US$5.65 million) in libel damages after a political opponent branded them liars.

The ruling drew criticism of Singapore's legal system by several analysts in Asia who pointed to sharp contrasts between Singapore's legal climate and courts in some of its neighbours such as Hong Kong, Japan, Malaysia, Taiwan and the Philippines.

"I feel very sorry for Singapore because all of their economic progress is not matched by progress in political maturity and liberties," said Nelson Navarro, a well-known Philippine political analyst and columnist.

"In the Philippines talk is cheap, there is virtually no libel in this country. We believe repression will inflict damage on other parts of the body politic. Filipinos can criticise their president but in Singapore they have to check their feelings."
A member of Hong Kong's Bar Council said the award seemed "very large" compared with cases in Hong Kong or Britain -- which share a Common Law-based legal system with Singapore.

"We don't seem to have these kinds of cases here and, in any event, damages that have been awarded in the few defamation cases we're looking at during the past few years don't seem to be on anything like the same scale," said Philip Dykes of the council, which represents the British territory's barristers.
"The English courts have said that when you get to such record amounts of damages you're beginning to put curbs on freedom of expression because it will have a chilling effect."
The situation with libel and defamation judgments in Hong Kong was unlikely to change after the territory reverts to Chinese rule on July 1, he added.
But Indian lawyers cheered the ruling, saying it was a bold decision which could provide a model.

"It is a very good judgment particularly when a lot of irresponsible criticism or defamation takes place of people in power or position, or those who have acquired some fame," said Duli Chand Singhania, a senior Delhi lawyer.

Such a case would unlikely find its way into Japan, mainly because lawmakers are immune from libel about statements made in parliament and unless it's an outrageous case outside parliament, few bother to bring such matters to Japan's snail-paced court system, Japanese legal experts said.
Japanese damage penalties are relatively minimal, they added.
Analysts in Taiwan noted that Singapore's ruling came a month after a Taiwan court acquitted four journalists in a libel suit brought by the powerful business chief of Taiwan's ruling party.

They said the contrasting verdicts showed that Taiwan values free speech more than its ethnic Chinese kin in Singapore -- but were quick to add that tolerance comes at the expense of social order in Taiwan's rambunctious democracy.
"In Taiwan you can pretty much say anything against the government and get away with it," said Chang Lin-chen, a law professor at National Taiwan University.

Singapore's Justice Chao Hick Tin, in a written judgment, ruled opposition politician Tang Liang Hong had made "malicious" attacks on Goh, former prime minister Lee Kuan Yew and the others which could have affected "their moral authority to govern".
Goh and his colleagues had demanded aggravated damages of S$12.9 million, arguing that Tang continued to defame them in media interviews which he gave after fleeing Singapore.
Tang, who fled to the south Malaysian state of Johor after losing a bitterly contested general election fight in January, told Reuters that he would appeal against the damages.
The award could also reinforce fears about whether booming Southeast Asia could sustain its dynamism, said one economist.

"Up to a certain stage you can separate economic reform from political reform, but we have come to a stage where political reform is a precondition for sustaining economic growth," said the economist, who declined to be identified.
Leaders in neighbouring Malaysia were quiet after the ruling.
Asked to comment on the court decision, an official at the Southeast Asia desk of Malaysia's Foreign Ministry said Malaysia does not comment on internal issues of another country.

Malaysia strictly enforces libel laws, and last month found an opposition politician guilty of sedition over a pamphlet he had published criticising the handling of a sex scandal involving a former chief minister of Malacca state.
Lim Guan Eng, deputy secretary-general of the Democratic Action Party (DAP), was fined 15,000 ringgit (US$6,000) and will be jailed for nine months if he does not pay.

"The judgement of guilt is expected. It's only to be expected that the Singaporean courts will always side with government," said George Aruta, opinion editor of the top selling Philippine Daily Inquirer.
